what_its_for: Entrectinib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of tumors. It works in adults and children (12 years and older) who have a specific gene change (called an NTRK fusion) in their solid tumors that has spread or cannot be removed by surgery. It is also used in adults with a type of lung cancer called ROS1-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread to other parts of the body.
how_to_take: Take entrectinib by mouth once a day, with or without food. Swallow the capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or open them. Try to take it at the same time each day. If you vomit after taking your dose, do not take another dose that day. Just take your next regular dose the following day.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 600 mg (three 200 mg capsules) taken by mouth once daily. For children 12 years and older, the dose is based on body weight and will be determined by your doctor. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions for your dose. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if your next scheduled dose is more than 12 hours away. If it is less than 12 hours until your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store entrectinib capsules at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the capsules in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Protect from moisture. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges (often found in marmalade) while taking this medicine, as they can increase the amount of drug in your body and raise the risk of side effects. Avoid taking strong medications that affect liver enzymes (CYP3A inducers or inhibitors) without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first — examples include rifampin, St. John's Wort, ketoconazole, and clarithromycin. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy, confused, or have vision problems. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 5 weeks after the last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: chest pain, shortness of breath, or a fast or irregular heartbeat (signs of heart problems); sudden numbness, weakness, confusion, severe headache, or trouble walking (signs of a possible stroke or nervous system problem); blurred vision, double vision, or other vision changes; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; signs of serious infection such as fever, chills, or unusual fatigue; broken bones or unusual bone or joint pain; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; mood changes, memory problems, or confusion; or swelling in your hands, feet, or legs.
when_it_works: Your doctor will monitor how well the medicine is working with regular check-ups, imaging scans, and lab tests. Some patients begin to see benefits within the first few months of treatment, but results vary from person to person. It is important to keep taking the medicine every day as prescribed, even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. Do not use during pregnancy. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 5 weeks after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use birth control during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 7 days after the last dose. Liver problems: If you have moderate to severe liver disease, your doctor may need to lower your dose. Kidney problems: Dose changes are usually not needed for mild to moderate kidney disease, but let your doctor know about any kidney problems. Children under 12: This medicine is not approved for children under 12 years old. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to certain side effects, such as dizziness or falls, and should be monitored carefully.
